hints: Notice the question asks about a stationary wave with fixed nodes of zero displacement and antinodes of maximum displacement.
Recall that two adjacent nodes, and also two adjacent antinodes, are separated by half a wavelength $\lambda/2$.
Compare each listed distance to $\lambda$ by doubling or halving $\lambda/2$ and $\lambda/4$ to see which gives a full $\lambda$.
walkthrough: Picture one loop of the stationary wave on the string: it runs from one node to the next adjacent node, with an antinode in the middle.
The physical rule for stationary waves is that adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, adjacent antinodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, and a node to an adjacent antinode is $\lambda/4$ apart.
Therefore the distance between adjacent antinodes on its own is $\lambda/2$, not the full wavelength.
The other options give $\lambda/4$: half the node-to-node distance is $\lambda/4$, and node to adjacent antinode is $\lambda/4$.
So double the distance between adjacent antinodes equals the wavelength. This is option A.

options.A: Adjacent antinodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, so twice that separation equals one full wavelength $\lambda$.
options.B: Adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, so half that distance is $\lambda/4$, not $\lambda$.
options.C: The distance between adjacent antinodes is only $\lambda/2$, which is half a wavelength.
options.D: A node to its adjacent antinode is a quarter-wave separation, equal to $\lambda/4$.
